newsitem.title: CHINA: No progress in talks over North Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: No progress in talks over North Korean defector.

text.p: South Korea and China on Thursday discussed the fate of the most senior North Korean official to flee the hermit Stalinist state but no progress was reported.

"It's still going on," South Korean embassy spokesman Chang Moon-ik said of the talks on Hwang Jang-yop, Pyongyang's top ideological theoretician who walked into Seoul's mission in Beijing on February 12 and has been marooned there ever since.
"Not this month," Chang said when asked if Hwang would be able to leave China in February.
The spokesman declined to say whether the defector would be permitted to leave next month. "It's very hard to say when this case will be over," he said.
The spokesman refused to say what issues, if any, were holding up negotiations.
South Korea's Defence Ministry said on Thursday, meanwhile that a North Korean woman had defected to South Korea across the demilitarised zone bisecting the Korean peninsula.
The ministry said the woman was in her 20s but gave no other details. Her motives for fleeing were being investigated.
Hwang has been stranded in Seoul's mission in Beijing since he plunged ties between China and the two rival Koreas into crisis by seeking asylum there.

The death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19 put negotiations over Hwang's fate largely on hold, but six days of mourning for the Chinese patriarch ended with his funeral on Tuesday.
The negotiations resumed in Beijing on Wednesday.
Spokesman Chang said the South had no plans to discuss the crisis with the North.
"We don't have any plan to contact North Korea because this should be solved between South Korea and the Chinese government," he said.

Chinese police backed by armoured personnel carriers and a riot truck maintained a tight guard around the Seoul consulate on a cold, grey Thursday, sealing off surrounding streets in the placid tree-lined embassy district.
Vanloads of police kept a close watch on Pyongyang's embassy a few kilometres (miles) away.
Hwang's defection has entangled China in the enmity between Seoul and Pyongyang, forcing Beijing to choose between its old communist comrades and its new capitalist partner.
Analysts say China will in the end almost certainly allow Hwang, architect of North Korea's governing ideology of strict self-reliance, to go to Seoul.
But Beijing also wants to help its Stalinist neighbour save face by being seen to give Pyongyang's concerns due attention.

Hwang's defection threw extra strain on ties between the two Koreas -- still technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce -- but there have been signs in recent days that the crisis may be easing.
Pyongyang, which at first insisted that Hwang had been kidnapped by South Korean agents, softened its stance last week by vowing to dismiss the ideologue if he had in fact defected.
